← Water softener bid calculator

How much to charge to install a water softener

The number a homeowner wants is a published “$799 installed” water-softener special, or a price they saw for a garage hang on a coupon site. That number is not a takeoff. A 32k PEX hang with ten included feet is not the same job as a 64k copper cut-in with an iron filter, a 40-foot brine drain, haul-away of the old unit, and a brine-tank receptacle. The trip is the same. The hours are not.

Open the free bid calculator

Count the extra pipe and the copper, not just the hang

Well-pump calculators price drop-pipe footage, a pitless, and a VFD. Water-heater calculators price a vent, a gas upsize, and an attic. Septic-pumping calculators price a tank lid, a hose, and extra gallons. A water-softener job is a water-treatment install: the unit, the run from the main, how the pipe is cut in, and the iron or RO that is not in the coupon. Quoting all of that from a published special is how the first soldered cut-in eats the field margin.

A job with the same trip can cost much more

Each extra foot past the included run is time that never appears on the coupon. Copper is billed as its own hours and material. An iron filter, a long brine drain, haul-away, and a brine receptacle are adders that get forgotten on a brochure special. On the sample rates a 64k salt unit with an iron filter, 45 feet of copper, a long drain, haul-away, and a receptacle prices about $4,968 ($110 per foot of pipe, 12.3 crew-hours). The same shop’s 32k PEX hang-only special prices about $1,318 ($165 per foot, 2.9 hours, walk-away $856). Matching the brochure job’s $799 special on the copper-and-iron house is how that job becomes a loss — the walk-away on the heavy job is already $3,229.

A salt-free copper run is not automatically the cheap one

A salt-free TAC unit with 40 feet of copper and no brine drain is not the 32k PEX special minus 100%. On the sample rates that salt-free job prices about $2,150 ($54 per foot, 7.2 crew-hours) — more than the brochure hang, not because TAC is slower but because 30 extra feet of copper do not live in a published garage special. A 48k salt unit with a copper cut-in, 25 extra feet, and haul-away prices about $2,601 (7.4 hours). Treating either as a blended add-on is how the special that looked fine turns into a loss after the first soldered run.

Load the wage, then keep a walk-away number

A $42/h tech loaded at 32% payroll burden is $55.44. Margin is a share of the price you send, not a markup on cost. The walk-away price is total cost — below that the job makes nothing before you take a dollar home. Replace every rate with your invoices before you send either number.

What this is not

This is not a water-quality report, a treatment specification, a building-code determination, a permit, an engineering stamp, or a recommended market price. It is arithmetic on the numbers you type. Grain capacity, hardness, pipe material, drain, and whether an iron filter is required are yours to confirm.

Price your water-softener job

Common questions

How much to charge to install a water softener?

Charge from the trip, the hang, extra pipe past the included run, copper versus PEX, grain capacity, iron or RO, the brine drain, haul-away, loaded labor, overhead, and a margin that is a share of price. A default 32k salt/resin PEX garage hang that stays inside the included footage, at the sample rates in this calculator, prices around $1,318 — about $165 per foot of pipe run.

Why is a $799 water-softener special dangerous?

Homeowners count the hang. Extra pipe, copper cut-in, an iron filter, a long brine drain, haul-away of the old unit, and a brine receptacle do not scale with that number. Matching a cheaper special written for a 32k PEX garage hang is how a 64k copper-and-iron job becomes a half-day loss.

How much to charge to install a water softener and iron filter?

A softener-and-iron job is not a hang-only special. On the sample rates a 64k salt unit with an iron filter, 45 feet of copper, a long drain, haul-away, and a brine receptacle prices around $4,968 ($110 per foot, 12.3 crew-hours), while a 32k PEX hang-only special prices around $1,318 ($165 per foot, 2.9 hours).

No warranty. This page and the calculator are free and as-is. They are not plumbing, water-treatment, construction, legal, tax, or financial advice. You are responsible for verifying every figure before you rely on it or send a bid.

      Hand the customer a proposal

      The price above is for you. This is the page you print or save as a PDF and give to the customer — your details, their details, the scope, the deposit split, and a line for them to sign. Your business details are saved on this device so you only type them once; the customer’s details are never saved.

      Everything on the printed page is text you typed or a number this calculator worked out. It contains no warranty, lien, or cancellation wording — those depend on your jurisdiction and your contract, and this tool is not the place to invent them.

      Common questions

      Why are the pipe and drain lines $0 when I entered lengths?

      Because both defaults sit inside their allowances. The base install carries 10 ft of supply pipe and 15 ft of drain line; the defaults enter 8 ft and 6 ft, so neither has chargeable extra footage and the $1.20 and $1.40 per-foot rates never engage. Enter a 25-foot drain run to a distant standpipe and the difference starts billing.

      Then why is there still a $35 drain material line?

      Because the drain kit is not the same thing as drain footage. The air gap, standpipe fitting, and clamps ship as a fixed kit whether the run is two feet or twenty — that is the $35, alongside a $65 bypass valve. Footage bills on top of it, not instead of it.

      Why doesn’t a 35% target margin mean marking cost up 35%?

      Because a margin is a share of the price, not an addition to the cost. The default install costs $856.42, and keeping 35% of the price means $856.42 ÷ 0.65 = $1,317.56. Marking the cost up by 35% would give $1,156.16, which is only a 25.9% margin — a $161 shortfall on a job this size, and proportionally the same on every job you price that way.

      What is deliberately not in this number?

      A water test, a permit, and haul-away of the old unit are all off or zero on the defaults, as is any electrical work and reverse-osmosis or iron-filter equipment. The estimate also assumes an existing loop to tie into. Sizing the unit to actual grains-per-gallon hardness is a judgment call this page does not make for you — the capacity selector is your input, not a recommendation.

Usage counts are anonymous tallies of which features were used, stored locally, and never include your footage, wages, costs, or prices.

vs-a-flat-rate-water-softener-special.ht.text:
← Water Softener Bid Calculator

This calculator vs. a flat-rate water-softener special

"$799 water softener installed" is not a price for a softener install — it is a price for one specific capacity, pipe run, and material, quietly applied to every house the truck pulls up to.

What a flat water-softener special is

A flat special is the fastest way to quote: one headline number on a postcard, a website, or a big-box flyer, read off and repeated. Homeowners shop it because it is easy to compare between bids, and it is the number a customer holding a competitor's flyer will ask you to match.

The number behind it was set for one job — one capacity, one pipe material, pipe and drain runs inside a fixed included footage, no iron filter, no RO, no haul-away — and then reused for every softener afterward, whether or not the next house looks anything like the one the rate was built on.

What this calculator is

This page keeps no account and sends nothing to a server. You enter the grain capacity, salt versus salt-free system, softener-only versus an iron filter or under-sink RO add-on, pipe material and run length past the included footage, the brine drain run, haul-away, and a brine receptacle, plus your loaded labor and overhead. It prices the pipe, the drain, and the extra-work hours separately, and returns a walk-away price and a price per extra foot of pipe — for this house, not a generic one.

What a flat special doesWhat this calculator does instead
Charges the same headline price whether the job is a 32k PEX garage hang with ten included feet or a 64k copper cut-in with an iron filter, a long drain, and haul-away — a several-times difference in labor and material for the same word "softener". Prices the pipe and drain from the entered run length, material, and included footage, so the two jobs above come out at different numbers instead of one.
Prices "a softener" as one hang, with no separate line for a soldered copper cut-in versus a PEX tie-in, or for an iron filter and under-sink RO added on top. Times the copper-versus-PEX labor and the iron-filter or RO install as their own hours, so that work shows up instead of being absorbed into the base price or skipped.
Assumes the old unit stays and no new circuit is needed, so a job that needs haul-away or a brine receptacle gets quoted the same as one that does not. Adds a haul-away and brine-receptacle line only when that scope is turned on, so the two jobs price differently.
Bakes payroll burden into a round "labor rate" nobody re-derives, so the rate quietly drifts from the crew's real loaded cost. Loads the entered hourly wage by the entered payroll-burden percentage every time, so labor cost tracks the actual burden rather than a memorized rate.
Gives the tech a price to quote, not a number to check a quote against when an owner asks to match a cheaper number. Reports the walk-away price and the price per foot of pipe, so a shopped price can be scored against real cost before the tech commits to it.

A flat special is not wrong because it is simple — it is wrong when it is applied outside the one job it was built for, and nothing about a postcard rate tells you when that has happened. This calculator does not replace judgment about your market; it replaces the arithmetic a flat rate skips.

Common questions

Why does a flat water-softener special get the price wrong?

Because the pipe, drain, and labor scale with the run length, the pipe material, and the work package, not with the word "softener" alone. A 32k PEX garage hang with ten included feet of pipe is a different job from a 64k copper cut-in with an iron filter, a long brine drain, and haul-away of the old unit. A flat special quotes both the same and is wrong on one of them every time.

What does a flat special usually leave out entirely?

Extra pipe and drain footage past whatever the special's fine print includes, the difference between a PEX tie-in and a soldered copper cut-in, and any iron filter or under-sink RO the homeowner adds on. A rate built around "install a softener" has nowhere to put those hours, so a tech pricing off the special alone is short before the truck is loaded.

What happens when haul-away or a brine receptacle gets added too?

A flat installed rate assumes the old unit stays put and no new circuit is needed. Hauling away the existing softener or running a receptacle for the control head is its own material and labor that a rate never asked about charges the same price for a job that takes longer and costs more.

Is a flat rate ever the right way to quote a softener install?

For a narrow band of near-identical jobs — same capacity, same pipe material, pipe and drain runs inside the included footage, no iron filter, no haul-away — a flat rate can land close. The risk is applying it outside that band without noticing, because the postcard rate does not know which band a given house is in and neither does the tech until the walkthrough.

Does this calculator know what to charge in my market?

No. It has no data on local rates, equipment cost, or what competitors charge. It takes the capacity, system, work package, pipe material and run, and your loaded labor and overhead, and turns them into a walk-away price and cost breakdown for the job you describe — the arithmetic a flat rate skips, not a market survey.

Nothing here says or implies that quoting a flat water-softener special is a bad-faith practice — it is a common, honest shortcut that works until the job stops matching the one the rate was set on. This page describes where that shortcut breaks down, not a fault in anyone who uses it.

Open the Water Softener Bid Calculator and price your own job.

No warranty. This free page is not plumbing, water-treatment, construction, legal, tax, or financial advice, and it does not tell you what to charge or whether a job may be built. Verify every figure against your own costs and a qualified, licensed professional before relying on it or submitting a bid. Whether an iron filter, RO, or haul-away is warranted is a judgment call for the licensed tech on site, not this page. This calculator vs. Jobber

Two different shapes: Jobber is an account-based platform for running a plumbing or water-treatment company's whole operation, including scheduling the crew and invoicing the customer once a job is priced. This page is a free, private worksheet for one question — what should this water-softener install cost, before you offer it.

What each tool is for

Jobber is a field service management platform used by home service businesses — plumbing, HVAC, lawn care, cleaning and general contracting among them — to run client management and online quoting, scheduling and crew dispatch, invoicing and online payments, and a client-facing hub, tied to one account used on an ongoing basis across every job the company runs. Jobber's own site is not reachable from this session to confirm today's specific feature list, plan names, or pricing, so only its well-documented identity and category are stated here: nothing about it is invented, and no dollar figure for it appears on this page. Public descriptions of that kind of field service software describe scheduling, invoicing and collecting payment for a job once its scope and price already exist; none describe working out what a water-softener install should cost from grain capacity, pipe run, copper versus PEX, iron filtration and haul-away before you quote it — which is the one thing this calculator does.

This calculator does none of what Jobber does. It does not manage a client list, dispatch a crew across a season, or collect a payment. It takes a water-softener install — grain capacity, salt or salt-free system, softener-only or with an iron filter or under-sink RO, pipe material and extra footage past the included run, the brine drain, haul-away of the old unit and a brine receptacle — plus loaded crew wage, payroll burden, travel and equipment, and overhead, and turns that into the install price, the walk-away floor, the price per foot of extra pipe, the effective crew hourly rate and, if you already have a number on the table, a check of whether it clears your own break-even floor, plus a printable customer proposal. It runs free in any browser, keeps no account, and uploads nothing you type.

Should I use this calculator or Jobber?

They do different jobs, and a plumbing or water-treatment shop of any size will likely end up touching both.
